transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Start: 11:30am PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Mariana Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Gomez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (GreenLine CTO), Samir Patel (GreenLine ML), Dana Kim (GreenLine PM)

Summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Redwood walked GreenLine through Redwood Optimize features focused on batching + prefix/KV caching and how those translate into per-token cost reductions. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and batching windows, caching hit rates, TTLs, memory implications for KV cache, and fallback strategies for capacity-constrained scenarios. Agreed next steps: share pricing, run a pilot benchmark on customer traces, and iterate on cache configuration.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, uh thanks for joining, really appreciate you taking time. Quick intros? I'll be the AE on the account. Mariana is our SE who will lead the technical bits.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Hi all, Jordan here. We'll jump in—Samir's on the ML side and Dana is PM. We're mainly interested in lowering per-request costs and improving throughput for our content-m generation pipelines.
[00:26] Samir Patel: Hi, yeah our biggest pain rn is cost at scale and tail latency spikes during peak. We're evaluating dedicated vs hosted.
[00:34] Mariana Ruiz: Great, that's exactly what Optimize helps with—specifically batching, prefix/KV cache, and some quantization recommendations. We'll run through practical settings and cost models.
[00:46] Dana Kim: Curious about how much caching actually helps; we have a lot of repeated prefixes in templates.
[00:52] Mariana Ruiz: Perfect. We'll start with a quick model of the numbers and then show the Console. So first a mental model: cost per user request ~= base per-token compute cost * tokens generated; batching multiplies throughput by increasing effective token utilization; caching reduces delta tokens that hit the model.
[01:15] Alex Chen: I'll share a small spreadsheet after the call but here's the high level: with a 40-60% prefix cache hit rate we've seen 20-35% net token cost reduction in customers similar to you. With aggressive batching (dynamic batching) you can get 1.8-2.4x throughput gains depending on request size distribution.
[01:33] Jordan Lee: Those numbers would be huge for us. How do you get that 40-60% cache hit? Our templates include user-specific fields so not all prefixes repeat exactly.
[01:43] Mariana Ruiz: Right, so we do prefix hashing and canonicalization: we canonicalize templated fields (like user_name -> <USER>) when customers provide templates. That increases logical cache hit. Also KV cache works well when you have conversational state or repeated instructions.
[02:02] Samir Patel: Does Redwood do manual canonicalization or we have to provide preprocessed prefixes? We want to avoid shipping PII.
[02:10] Priya Gomez: You can send anonymized traces. We also support client-side canonicalization patterns in the SDK so you don't have to send raw PII. The cache keys are hashed; we don't store raw prefix text in plaintext in the cache logs.
[02:24] Dana Kim: Ok good. Can you talk on the latency tradeoffs—we can't afford >200ms p95 for short queries.
[02:31] Mariana Ruiz: Totally. There's a tradeoff: batching introduces a micro-window to collect requests. If you set batch window = 25ms and you have enough QPS, you typically see 10-30% lower cost without pushing p95 over your threshold. For low QPS endpoints, we rely more on prefix/KV cache to reduce token volume, which is especially useful for short predictions.
[02:54] [03:00] Jordan Lee: What's the difference between prefix cache and KV cache?
[03:02] Mariana Ruiz: Good question. Prefix cache stores entire prefix+prompt outputs (think response tokens) for repeat requests—works great for near-identical prompts. KV cache stores model key-value attention caches for autoregressive decoding so when you re-use prefix states you avoid recomputing earlier layers—this is more memory intensive but enables very fast warm-starts in chat scenarios.
[03:24] Samir Patel: So KV cache is per-model and per-sequence length? Memory blow-up concerns?
[03:29] Mariana Ruiz: Yes, KV cache size scales roughly with model hidden size * sequence length * number of layers. We provide estimates in the Console; for example a 7B model with 2048 context and 32 layers is roughly X MB per active cache entry (we gave approximate numbers in the shared doc). For many customers we prune old entries and use LRU TTLs.
[03:50] Jordan Lee: You said prefix cache gives 20-35% cost improvement, batching gives 1.8-2.4x throughput. How do we combine them in a cost model?
[03:58] Mariana Ruiz: Combine multiplicatively in rough terms: Effective tokens = (1 - cache_hit_rate) * avg_tokens_per_request; Effective cost per request = base_cost_per_token * Effective tokens / batching_efficiency. So if you have 50% cache hit, avg 300 tokens, base cost $0.00002/token, and batching eff 2.0, cost = 0.00002 * (0.5*300)/2 = $0.0015 per request. Our Optimize calculator in the Console will run this against your trace to give a distribution and percentile costs.
[04:36] [04:45] Dana Kim: That formula helps. Are there examples from other media customers?
[04:48] Alex Chen: We shared a reference sheet in the deck—customers with template-heavy flows see cache hit rates up to 70% with careful canonicalization and that drove 30-50% cost savings. Other customers with high variability in prefixes rely more on KV caching + batching.
[05:05] Samir Patel: What about cold starts: if a user hits a unique prompt, is there a big hit?
[05:09] Mariana Ruiz: Cold-starts are always the worst case; however, prefix cache warm-up is quick if you have recurring content. We also support async pre-warming: if you know a campaign will start at 10am you can pre-warm popular prefixes during off-peak hours to populate the cache.
[05:26] Jordan Lee: How do you measure cache hit rate?
[05:29] Mariana Ruiz: In Console we show token-level breakdowns and a cache dashboard that reports hit/miss by endpoint and TTL bucket. We also provide suggestions—if 20% of requests are 80/20 prefixes we may recommend grouping certain templates or increasing TTL.
[05:45] [06:00] Priya Gomez: Quick demo—I'm going to share the Console. Note: screen may say sample data.
[06:05] [06:10] Priya Gomez (screen share): On the Optimize tab we have a Batching panel and Cache panel. Here is a histogram of request token counts; here's a slider to set batch window in ms and an estimated batching multiplier shown next to it. If I move the window from 10ms to 50ms you see the estimated latency increase at p95 but batching improves from 1.3x to 1.9x.
[06:34] Samir Patel: Can you explain the batching multiplier?
[06:37] Priya Gomez: It's basically expected effective tokens processed per GPU run divided by average tokens per single-request run. We estimate it from your QPS and token distribution. It's stochastic, so we provide conservative and optimistic estimates.
[06:50] Jordan Lee: What's the latency penalty for 50ms window? For short requests that might double p95.
[06:56] Mariana Ruiz: Often the added latency is the batching window plus queueing; so if p95 target is 200ms and average generation is 60ms, adding a 50ms window may push p95 toward 110-130ms dependent on concurrency; it's not necessarily doubling, unless your base generation is small. The Console gives simulated p95.
[07:18] Dana Kim: What about fallback behavior if we lose dedicated capacity? We need graceful degradation.
[07:22] Alex Chen: Good—we do smart routing: requests can fall back to compatible smaller models, different regions, or hosted pool tiers, with config for quality thresholds. Reducing model size and leveraging caching can keep the experience up while reducing cost.
[07:35] Samir Patel: Are there any security implications for storing cache keys or pre-warmed prefixes?
[07:41] Mariana Ruiz: Cache keys are hashed. For Private customers we can enable KMS/HSM control; audit logs record cache access. SOC2/ISO compliance and SSO/SAML support available—these are standard enterprise options.
[07:54] [08:00] Jordan Lee: Can Optimize recommendations be automated? We don't want to manually tune windows.
[08:03] Mariana Ruiz: Yes, Optimize includes recommendation engine: given traces it will propose batch window, TTL, and quantization profile. You can choose automated apply or manual review. We also offer conservative defaults for production.
[08:17] Samir Patel: Quantization recommendations—are those quality-risky?
[08:20] Mariana Ruiz: We recommend per-workload quantization. For many generation tasks 4-bit or 8-bit quantization has negligible quality impact but large cost savings. We run regression tests tied to eval prompts you supply. If there's a regression, we fail the rollout.
[08:37] Dana Kim: Could you walk through a worked example for our workloads?
[08:40] Mariana Ruiz: Sure. If your traces show avg tokens generated = 250, average prefix tokens = 80, and 30% of prefixes repeat, then effective tokens = (1 - 0.3) * 250 = 175. If batching gets you 2x efficiency, that's equivalent to 87.5 tokens worth of compute per logical request. Using a base per-token compute price of $0.000025 gives ~ $0.0022 per request. If you push cache hit to 50% that's $0.0014 per request. We'll put your actual numbers into the Optimize calculator and provide a distribution.
[09:18] [09:30] Jordan Lee: These per-request dollars look good. Can you show how memory sizing for KV cache will affect our Dedicated cluster sizing?
[09:35] Mariana Ruiz: Absolutely. The Console's Capacity planner has a KV cache memory estimator. Example: if you plan for 10k active chat sessions with avg context 1024 tokens on a 7B model, that implies roughly Y GB of KV memory—so you'd want to provision that into Dedicated pool with autoscaling headroom. We can run these numbers for your actual expected concurrent sessions.
[09:58] Samir Patel: For autoscaling, is there an option to prefer cold starts rather than over-provisioning? We want to avoid paying for unused capacity.
[10:06] Alex Chen: Yes, you can configure a mixed policy: baseline reserved + burst-on-demand. For bursts we route to hosted pools automatically. That gives predictable throughput at baseline while keeping tail costs reasonable.
[10:19] [10:30] Dana Kim: Any gotchas regarding TTLs for cache entries? We worry about stale content in generative outputs.
[10:36] Mariana Ruiz: TTL is policy-driven. For templates with dynamic fields you may set short TTLs or use cache invalidation by key. We also support content-aware invalidation if you include a version hash in the prefix key.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: How long to run a pilot? We need credible numbers.
[10:53] Alex Chen: Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks. We prefer 1-2k samples + representative live routing at low percentage (1-5%) to measure real cache behavior. We'll help run the benchmark and provide a CSV with latency and cost breakdowns.
[11:05] Samir Patel: If we do a pilot, can Redwood sign a data processing addendum?
[11:09] Alex Chen: Yes, we have standard DPA + SOC2 docs; we'll include that in the package.
[11:14] [11:20] Priya Gomez: Quick note on tooling: the Console exposes per-route token histograms, a cache heatmap, and a batching simulator. You can also export the recommended config as JSON to apply via our API.
[11:30] Jordan Lee: One more on pricing: what's the delta between hosted and dedicated for per-token price?
[11:34] Alex Chen: Pricing varies by committed capacity and model family. Hosted is pay-as-you-go rate; Dedicated has commit discounts. We'll send a customized sheet—but typical committed discounts range from 20-40% depending on term/commit.
[11:46] Dana Kim: OK great. I think we have the info we need to decide on the pilot.
[11:50] Alex Chen: Excellent. Recap of next steps: we'll send pricing, Optimize deck, and run a benchmark if you share traces. Mariana will run the first pass of the benchmark and we'll reconvene to go over results.
[11:59] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone—this was helpful.
[12:01] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts and due dates. Bye all.

End transcript.
